contentHtml:
AFRICA – Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has invested more than US$30 million to install solar power in over 1,700 primary healthcare facilities across five countries in Africa and Asia, improving electricity access and immunisation services for more than 140 million people.

The initiative covers Ethiopia, Nigeria, Pakistan, Uganda and Zambia.

It addresses unreliable electricity supplies at frontline health facilities, which often disrupt vaccine storage, diagnostic services and access to essential healthcare, particularly in remote communities.

The milestone comes as governments, development partners, climate experts and civil society organisations meet at COP31 in Türkiye to discuss practical measures for strengthening community resilience and advancing climate and development objectives.

Solar power strengthens frontline healthcare

Unreliable electricity remains a major obstacle to equitable immunisation, particularly in rural and underserved areas.

Facilities located beyond national electricity grids often depend on expensive or inconsistent power supplies, limiting their ability to maintain vaccine cold chains and provide uninterrupted care.

Solar installations offer an alternative by providing reliable, lower-emission electricity.

They enable health workers to operate refrigerators, diagnostic equipment and other essential medical devices while extending service hours and supporting emergency care, including at night.

The programme has delivered different levels of investment across the five countries.

Nigeria accounts for the largest coverage, with 371 solar-powered primary healthcare facilities serving an estimated 115 million people through approximately US$9 million in funding.

Ethiopia has solarised 380 facilities, benefiting around 8.6 million people through US$6.39 million in investment.

In Pakistan, US$6.67 million has supported solar installations in 398 facilities, extending healthcare access to approximately 12.4 million people.

Uganda has upgraded 250 facilities through US$4.25 million in funding, reaching an estimated 3.1 million people.

Meanwhile, Zambia has solarised 296 facilities, improving access to healthcare for approximately 1.3 million people through US$4.17 million in support.

Cold chain investments support vaccine delivery

Beyond powering healthcare facilities, reliable electricity is essential for maintaining vaccines at recommended temperatures.

Power interruptions can expose vaccines to damaging heat, resulting in wastage and disruptions to immunisation programmes.

Gavi has invested in cold chain infrastructure across lower-income countries for more than two decades.

Its support has included the deployment of over 66,400 solar direct-drive (SDD) vaccine refrigerators, which operate using solar energy to maintain vaccine storage temperatures.

These refrigerators are projected to prevent up to 153,024 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions over their 10-year operational lifespan.

The investment also reduces reliance on conventional electricity and diesel-powered refrigeration in areas with limited energy infrastructure.

Commenting on the initiative, Ian MacTavish, Director of Vaccine Forecasting and Supply Management at Gavi, said investment in solar power at primary healthcare facilities was addressing a critical barrier to vaccine equity while helping countries develop more resilient and sustainable health systems.

He noted that solar-powered clinics help preserve vaccine quality, support consistent healthcare delivery and improve access to essential services in remote communities.
